ddx.step1_summary:
- Chief complaint: Lower central abdominal (tummy) pain for ~2 days.
- Symptoms:
  - Location: just below the belly button (suprapubic/midline lower abdomen).
  - Onset/duration: Gradual onset about 2 days ago; getting a bit worse; fairly constant.
  - Quality/severity: Burning type pain; sore to pressure; patient can still move and function.
  - Associated: Mild nausea, feeling hot and sweaty (subjective feverish); noticed "pink" urine (possible blood); increased urinary frequency (patient attributes to high fluid intake); no dysuria (no burning when passing urine), no vomiting, bowels: recent constipation last week now improved, current bowel movements normal.
  - Gynaecologic: Sexually active with one partner; Implanon implant placed ~1 year ago; last sexual activity 4 days ago; last period ~2 weeks ago; last STI screen normal 6 months ago.
- Past medical history: Reported generally fit and well; no surgeries.
- Medications / Allergies: Only contraception: Implanon; no other medications reported; no allergies mentioned.
- Family / Social history: No relevant family history reported; lives in a share house with roommates; works as an accountant; non-smoker; drinks socially.
- Vital signs / Exam findings: No formal vitals recorded. Subjective feeling hot/sweaty. On exam, patient reports suprapubic tenderness ("sore when I press on it"). No other exam details documented.
- Labs / Imaging: None performed yet. Doctor discussed urine testing and pregnancy test and empirically prescribed trimethoprim (2 tablets, one twice daily for 3 days).

V: Ovarian torsion: Torsion can cause acute lower abdominal/pelvic pain with nausea and tenderness; vascular compromise of an adnexal structure could present with sudden or gradual worsening pain.
Ureteric/renal stone causing hematuria: Stones can cause pain and frank or microscopic hematuria (patient noted pink urine) and lower abdominal/groin pain.
I: Acute lower urinary tract infection (cystitis): Frequency and pink urine with suprapubic burning pain and tenderness are consistent; physician empirically treated for UTI.
Pyelonephritis: Systemic symptoms (fever, sweats, nausea) occur, but classical flank pain/back pain and severe systemic illness are not described.

Pelvic inflammatory disease (PID) / tubo-ovarian abscess: Sexually transmitted infection/inflammation can cause lower abdominal pain and systemic symptoms; less likely given monogamous partner and recent normal STI screen but still possible.
N: Ovarian cyst or hemorrhagic cyst: Can cause acute pelvic pain, midline or unilateral, sometimes with localized tenderness; may cause internal bleeding leading to blood being noticed (vaginal vs urinary).
Pelvic mass (less likely acute): Unlikely to present abruptly over 2 days in an otherwise well young patient but included for completeness.
D: Constipation-related pain/impaction: Patient had constipation last week which is improving; retained stool can cause lower abdominal discomfort.
Irritable bowel syndrome flare: Could present with lower abdominal discomfort but typically with chronic pattern and altered bowel habits.
I2: Side effect of Implanon: Hormonal implant can cause irregular bleeding and pelvic discomfort; bleeding could be mistaken as pink urine if contamination occurs.
Antibiotic/medication reaction (not applicable yet): No recent new drugs except Implanon; currently being prescribed trimethoprim.
C: Congenital urinary tract anomaly with recurrent urinary symptoms: Could predispose to UTIs or hematuria, but no history to suggest this.
A: Endometriosis (cyclical pelvic pain): Typically chronic and cyclical; less likely for acute 2-day onset but can present with localized pelvic pain.
Allergic/local inflammatory reaction (rare): Not suggested by history.
T: Trauma to abdomen/pelvis: No history of trauma reported.
E: Ectopic pregnancy / early pregnancy complications: Pregnancy-related causes (ectopic, threatened miscarriage) can cause lower abdominal pain and bleeding; Implanon reduces but does not eliminate pregnancy risk—patient reports possible pink urine and last period ~2 weeks ago.
Metabolic causes (e.g., diabetic ketoacidosis): No supporting history (no polyuria beyond fluid intake, no known diabetes).

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Suprapubic burning pain and tenderness, new urinary frequency, and discoloured (pink) urine are classic for lower UTI. The physician also considered and empirically treated for UTI, which reflects clinical probability.
supporting_evidence: Burning suprapubic pain localized below the belly button
Pink-coloured urine (possible hematuria) noted by patient
Mild nausea and subjective feverish/sweaty feeling
opposing_evidence: No dysuria / no explicit burning on urination reported
Urine testing/result not yet available to confirm infection

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Hematuria (pink urine) plus lower abdominal pain can be seen with urinary tract stones. Pain from stones can be localized to lower abdomen if the stone is distal; nausea is a common associated symptom.
opposing_evidence: Pain character described as constant burning rather than severe colicky pain typical of ureteric stones
No reported severe acute radiating flank-to-groin pain
No microscopic hematuria or imaging to confirm

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Gynecologic cause — ectopic pregnancy or ovarian pathology (ruptured cyst/ovarian torsion)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Lower central pelvic pain, nausea, and possible bleeding (pink fluid) could represent a gynecologic cause. Although Implanon reduces pregnancy risk, ectopic pregnancy remains possible. Ovarian cyst rupture or torsion can present with acute pelvic pain and tenderness.
supporting_evidence: Location of pain in lower pelvis/suprapubic area
Pain is tender to palpation and getting worse
Reported pink discoloration noted (could represent bleeding)
opposing_evidence: Patient on Implanon (lowers pregnancy risk) and reports recent normal STI screen
No vaginal bleeding explicitly described (pink urine may not be vaginal blood)
No unilateral severe adnexal pain or sudden severe pain typical of torsion described
No syncope/hypotension or severe acute presentation that would suggest rupture with significant intraperitoneal bleeding

step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: PID can cause lower abdominal pain, systemic symptoms, and pelvic tenderness. It is less likely given monogamous partner and recent normal STI screen, and absence of abnormal vaginal discharge or higher fever.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal pain and systemic symptoms (sweats, nausea)
opposing_evidence: Recent STI screen normal 6 months ago and single partner since
No significant fever or marked systemic illness described

step3_ranked_ddx.diagnosis: Constipation / gastrointestinal cause (including early appendicitis or IBS)
step3_ranked_ddx.explanation: Patient had constipation last week (now improved), and bowel-origin pain can present in the lower abdomen. However current bowel movements are normal and pain quality/location favors urinary or gynecologic causes.
supporting_evidence: Lower abdominal pain could be referred from bowel
opposing_evidence: Bowel habit now reported as normal and no diarrhoea or bloody stools
Pain described as burning and suprapubic which is more typical of urinary/gynecologic origin
